question.prompt: Triangle I is equilateral with side \(A,\) perimeter \(P,\) area \(K,\) and circumradius \(R\) (radius of the circumscribed circle). Triangle II is equilateral with side \(a,\) perimeter \(p,\) area \(k,\) and circumradius \(r.\) If \(A\) is different from \(a,\) then:

solutions.explanation:
All equilateral triangles have three \(60^\circ\) angles, so the two triangles are similar. Let
\[
t=\frac{A}{a}.
\]
Because side lengths are positive and \(A\ne a\), we have \(t>0\) and \(t\ne1\).

Changing from triangle II to triangle I multiplies every length by \(t\), so their perimeters satisfy \(P/p=t\). The same change of scale takes the circumcircle of triangle II to the circumcircle through the corresponding vertices of triangle I. Its radius is also multiplied by \(t\), so \(R/r=t\). Consequently,
\[
\frac{P}{p}=\frac{R}{r}=t
\]
always.

Areas have the square of the length scale factor: both a base and its corresponding height are multiplied by \(t\). Thus
\[
\frac{K}{k}=t^2.
\]
Since \(t>0\) and \(t\ne1\), we have \(t^2\ne t\). The stated equalities involving the area ratio therefore never hold for these two distinct side lengths. The correct choice is \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
solutions.title: Compare length and area scale factors
